---
title: "ipw and WeightIt side by side"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_weightit <- requireNamespace("WeightIt", quietly = TRUE)
# Bootstrap standard errors (section 1), made once with
# data-raw/make-weightit-article-data.R
stored <- readRDS("ipw-and-weightit.rds")
```

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(ipw)
library(survival)
```

[WeightIt](https://ngreifer.github.io/WeightIt/) (Greifer) and ipw both
estimate weights for marginal structural models. This article runs the two
packages on the same data: a binary and a categorical point treatment,
where both apply and should give the same answer, and longitudinal data
with individual visit times, where they work differently. WeightIt is used
only through its exported functions. This page was built with ipw
`r packageVersion("ipw")``r if (has_weightit) paste0(" and WeightIt ", packageVersion("WeightIt"))`.

# 1. Binary point treatment

A confounder `l`, a binary covariate `x`, a binary treatment `a` and an
outcome `y`; the effect of `a` on `y` is 2 for everyone, so all estimands
are 2 in truth.

```{r binary-data}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 1000
d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n), x = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4))
d$a <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.3 + 0.8 * d$l + 0.5 * d$x))
d$y <- 2 * d$a + d$l + d$x + rnorm(n)
stopifnot(all.equal(sum(d$y), stored$data_check))   # same data as the bootstrap
```

## The weights

With a logistic model, both packages fit the same propensity score with
`glm()` and apply the same formulas, so the weights should agree up to
rounding:

```{r binary-weights, eval = has_weightit}
estimands <- c("ATE", "ATT", "ATC", "ATO")
w_ipw <- lapply(setNames(estimands, estimands), function(est)
  ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
           denominator = ~ l + x, data = d, estimand = est))
w_wit <- lapply(setNames(estimands, estimands), function(est)
  WeightIt::weightit(a ~ l + x, data = d, method = "glm", estimand = est))
sapply(estimands, function(est)
  c(max.abs.difference = max(abs(w_ipw[[est]]$ipw.weights - w_wit[[est]]$weights)),
    max.weight = max(w_ipw[[est]]$ipw.weights)))
```

The largest difference is at the level of floating-point rounding.
Stabilized ATE weights agree too: `numerator = ~ 1` in ipw and
`stabilize = TRUE` in WeightIt.

## Standard errors

The marginal structural model is the weighted regression of `y` on `a`.
Four standard errors of the coefficient of `a`:

* **ipwvcov()**: ipw's M-estimation standard error (new), which accounts
  for the estimation of the weights;
* **glm_weightit(vcov = "asympt")**: WeightIt's M-estimation standard error;
* **robust (HC0)**: the sandwich standard error that treats the weights as
  known, as `svyglm()` or `glm_weightit(vcov = "HC0")` give it;
* **bootstrap**: `r stored$R` bootstrap samples, re-estimating the weights
  in each (computed once, see the setup chunk).

```{r binary-se, eval = has_weightit}
se_table <- t(sapply(estimands, function(est) {
  msm <- lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = w_ipw[[est]]$ipw.weights)
  fit_m <- WeightIt::glm_weightit(y ~ a, data = d, weightit = w_wit[[est]], vcov = "asympt")
  fit_r <- WeightIt::glm_weightit(y ~ a, data = d, weightit = w_wit[[est]], vcov = "HC0")
  c(estimate = unname(coef(msm)["a"]),
    ipwvcov = sqrt(ipwvcov(w_ipw[[est]], msm)["a", "a"]),
    glm_weightit.asympt = sqrt(vcov(fit_m)["a", "a"]),
    robust.HC0 = sqrt(vcov(fit_r)["a", "a"]),
    bootstrap = unname(stored$boot_se[est]))
}))
round(se_table, 4)
```

`ipwvcov()` and `glm_weightit(vcov = "asympt")` agree to many decimals:
they solve the same stacked estimating equations (Lunceford & Davidian
2004). Both are close to the bootstrap. The robust standard error, which
ignores that the weights were estimated, is larger for all four estimands
here, so confidence intervals based on it would be wider than needed. For
the ATE this is the usual direction (estimating the weights reduces the
variance); for the ATT, ATC and ATO the robust standard error is not
guaranteed to be conservative and can also be too small. The M-estimation
or bootstrap standard error is therefore preferred.

`ipwvcov()` covers binary point treatments with `lm()` or `glm()` outcome
models. WeightIt's outcome-model functions cover more: multi-category and
continuous treatments, many weighting methods, Cox, ordinal and multinomial
outcome models, and longitudinal weights from `weightitMSM()`.

# 2. Categorical point treatment

A treatment with three levels, A, B and C. With `estimand = "ATT"` and a
**focal** level, people at that level keep weight 1 and the others are
reweighted to resemble them; `estimand = "ATO"` gives generalized overlap
weights (Li & Li 2019).

```{r cat-data}
set.seed(31)
n <- 1000
dc <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n), z = rnorm(n))
pr <- cbind(1, exp(0.5 + 0.8 * dc$l), exp(-0.3 - 0.6 * dc$l + 0.4 * dc$z))
pr <- pr / rowSums(pr)
dc$m <- factor(apply(pr, 1, function(p) sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 1, prob = p)))
table(dc$m)
```

```{r cat-weights, eval = has_weightit}
compare <- function(estimand, focal = NULL, ...) {
  wi <- ipwpoint(exposure = m, family = "multinomial", denominator = ~ l + z, data = dc,
                 estimand = estimand, focal = focal, ...)$ipw.weights
  ww <- WeightIt::weightit(m ~ l + z, data = dc, method = "glm",
                           estimand = estimand, focal = focal)$weights
  max(abs(wi / ww - 1))
}
rbind(
  default.multinom = c(ATT.focal.A = compare("ATT", "A"), ATO = compare("ATO")),
  tight.multinom = c(ATT.focal.A = compare("ATT", "A", reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000),
                     ATO = compare("ATO", reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000)))
```

The table shows the largest relative difference between the weights. ipw
fits the multinomial model with `nnet::multinom()`, which by default stops
when the relative change in the fit criterion falls below `1e-8`; that
leaves relative differences of up to about 1e-3 from WeightIt, whose own
fitter converges further. With a tighter tolerance (`reltol`, passed on
through `...`), the weights agree to about 1e-8: the formulas are the
same. Within each level,
the ATT weights make the covariate means resemble those of the focal group:

```{r cat-balance, eval = has_weightit}
w_att <- ipwpoint(exposure = m, family = "multinomial", denominator = ~ l + z,
                  data = dc, estimand = "ATT", focal = "A")$ipw.weights
rbind(unweighted = tapply(dc$l, dc$m, mean),
      ATT.focal.A = sapply(levels(dc$m), function(k)
        weighted.mean(dc$l[dc$m == k], w_att[dc$m == k])))
```

For an ordered exposure, ipw uses `MASS::polr()` (`family = "ordinal"`);
WeightIt also fits an ordinal model for an ordered factor. In the package
tests the two agree to 1e-4 or better.

# 3. Longitudinal data with individual visit times

Here the two packages are designed differently.

* `ipwtm()` works on **long data**: one row per person per interval between
  visits, with `tstart` and `timevar`. The exposure model is fitted once,
  pooled over all rows (a Cox model, a pooled logistic regression, or a
  multinomial, ordinal or GEE model), so each person can have their own
  number of visits at their own times.
* `weightitMSM()` works on **wide data**: one row per person, and one
  treatment model per time point, given in `formula.list`. Its help page
  states that only wide data are supported. The time points are therefore
  the same for everyone. The weight is the product of the weights at the
  time points. This fits designs with fixed visits, such as yearly
  measurements in a cohort or a trial with scheduled visits, and it allows
  any WeightIt method at each time point.

## Data with individual visit times

We simulate 1000 people followed for 5 years. Each person is seen at
their own times, about twice a year on average with random gaps. At each
visit a confounder `l` is measured; it depends on its previous value and on
treatment. People not yet treated may start treatment at a visit, more
likely when `l` is low. Once started, treatment continues.

```{r long-data}
set.seed(11)
n <- 1000
sim_person <- function(i) {
  t <- 0; l <- rnorm(1); a <- 0; l0 <- l; rows <- list()
  repeat {
    t_next <- t + rexp(1, rate = 2)           # gap to the next visit
    if (t_next > 5) break
    l <- 0.8 * l + 0.4 * a + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5)  # confounder measured at the visit
    start <- if (a == 0) rbinom(1, 1, plogis(-2.5 - 1.0 * l)) else 0
    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(id = i, tstart = t, time = t_next,
                                           l0 = l0, l = l, start = start)
    if (start == 1) a <- 1
    t <- t_next
  }
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), sim_person))
long$a <- ave(long$start, long$id, FUN = cummax)   # 1 from the visit of starting on
head(long[, c("id", "tstart", "time", "l", "a")], 4)
c(people = n, rows = nrow(long), started = sum(long$start))
summary(as.vector(table(long$id)))   # number of visits per person
```

## ipw: the long data as they are

`ipwtm()` fits a Cox model for the time to starting treatment on the
intervals between each person's own visits; with `type = "first"` the rows
after the start are not used for the model and keep the weight reached at
the start.

```{r long-ipw}
w_tm <- ipwtm(exposure = a, family = "survival", numerator = ~ l0,
              denominator = ~ l0 + l, id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = time,
              type = "first", data = long)
summary(w_tm$ipw.weights)
```

The weights can be used directly in a weighted model on the same rows, for
example `coxph(Surv(tstart, time, event) ~ a + l0, weights = w_tm$ipw.weights,
...)` for an outcome event.

## WeightIt: a common time grid first

For `weightitMSM()`, the data must first be put on time points that are
the same for everyone, say the end of each year. At each time point `k`,
the analyst has to choose a value of `l` and of the treatment. A common
choice is the last value observed up to `k` (the baseline value if there
was no visit yet) and "started by `k`":

```{r long-grid}
grid <- 1:5
last_before <- function(k, column, default) {
  sub <- long[long$time <= k, ]
  last <- sub[!duplicated(sub$id, fromLast = TRUE), ]   # rows are in time order
  out <- default
  out[last$id] <- last[[column]]
  out
}
l0 <- long$l0[!duplicated(long$id)]
wide <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n), l0 = l0)
for (k in grid) {
  wide[[paste0("L", k)]] <- last_before(k, "l", l0)
  wide[[paste0("A", k)]] <- last_before(k, "a", rep(0, n))
}
head(wide, 3)
```

One model per time point, each with the treatment history and the
confounder history up to then (here the previous treatment and current
`l`), and a numerator model with the treatment history and baseline `l0`:

```{r long-weightit, eval = has_weightit, warning = FALSE}
formulas <- lapply(grid, function(k)
  as.formula(if (k == 1) "A1 ~ l0 + L1" else
               sprintf("A%d ~ A%d + l0 + L%d", k, k - 1, k)))
num_formulas <- lapply(grid, function(k)
  as.formula(if (k == 1) "~ l0" else sprintf("~ A%d + l0", k - 1)))
w_msm <- WeightIt::weightitMSM(formulas, data = wide, method = "glm",
                               stabilize = TRUE, num.formula = num_formulas)
summary(w_msm$weights)
```

`glm()` warns here (warnings hidden) that fitted probabilities of 0 or 1
occurred: people who already started have `A(k-1) = 1` and therefore
`A(k) = 1`, so the model at each time point also "predicts" a treatment
that is no longer a choice; their factor is about 1. This matches what
`type = "first"` does in ipw by leaving those rows out of the model.

## What the grid means for such data

The grid analysis uses the data in a coarser form. How much is lost depends
on how far the visit times are from the grid:

```{r grid-cost}
starts <- long[long$start == 1, ]
grid_k <- ceiling(starts$time)                     # grid point at which the start is seen
l_at_grid <- mapply(function(i, k) wide[i, paste0("L", k)], starts$id, grid_k)
last_visit <- sapply(grid, function(k) {
  sub <- long[long$time <= k, ]
  mean(k - tapply(sub$time, sub$id, max))
})
c(visits.per.person = nrow(long) / n,
  grid.points.per.person = length(grid),
  starts.l.differs.from.l.at.start = mean(abs(l_at_grid - starts$l) > 1e-12),
  mean.years.between.last.visit.and.grid.point = mean(last_visit))
```

* **Timing.** About ten visits per person are reduced to five time points.
  A start at 1.1 and one at 1.9 years are both "started by year 2".
* **Which `l`.** For more than half of the people who started, the `l`
  used at the grid point is not the value measured at the visit where
  treatment was started. It
  comes from a later visit in the same year, measured *after* the start and
  so possibly affected by treatment, which the treatment model should not
  adjust for. Using the value at the start instead needs extra data
  preparation.
* **Carried-forward values.** On average the last visit was about half a
  year before the grid point, so for people who did not start, `l` is
  older than the time point it stands for.

A finer grid (for example monthly) reduces these problems, but means many
more time points with few or no visits, each with its own model and many
carried-forward values. Neither the grid analysis nor the long-data
analysis is wrong in general: with scheduled visits that everyone attends,
the grid is the design, and `weightitMSM()` offers the full range of
WeightIt methods at each time point. With visit times that differ between
people, `ipwtm()` uses each person's own intervals directly.

# 4. Which to use

* **WeightIt** for point treatments when you want machine-learning or
  balancing methods (GBM, SuperLearner, BART, CBPS, entropy balancing,
  energy balancing, ...), many estimands, balance diagnostics through cobalt
  and M-estimation standard errors for outcome models (`glm_weightit()`,
  `coxph_weightit()`, ...). Also for longitudinal treatments measured at
  fixed time points that are the same for everyone.
* **ipw** for exposures that change over time in long (counting-process)
  data with each person's own visit times; Cox models for the time to the
  first switch or to censoring (`ipwtm(family = "survival")`); exposures
  that switch back and forth or recur (`type = "all"`); count and skewed
  continuous exposures (Poisson, negative binomial, gamma, log-normal); and
  analyses with few dependencies.
* For a binary or categorical point treatment with a logistic model, the
  two give the same weights; for a binary one, `ipwvcov()` and
  `glm_weightit(vcov = "asympt")` give the same standard errors.

The [README](https://tranhung93.github.io/ipw/index.html#ipw-or-weightit)
has a comparison table.

* Lunceford JK, Davidian M (2004). Stratification and weighting via the
  propensity score in estimation of causal treatment effects: a comparative
  study. *Statistics in Medicine* 23, 2937–2960.
